## Abstract

In 2017, Ilya Prigogine would have been 100 years of age. As for any human being, this centenary is a notable event. For him, as a scientist, 2017 was also above all the 50th anniversary of dissipative structures. It was indeed in 1967 that for the first time he used this denomination at the occasion of an important scientific event and in publications. The attribution of this qualification for self-organized behaviours of matter only possible far from equilibrium coincided with the outcome of a research effort of more than 25 years. Centred in thermodynamics and statistical physics on the role played by irreversible processes in the physical evolution of matter, the aim of this research is clear from the outset of his scientific career. With visionary personal intuition and iron-willed determination, it was pursued. The road to success had been long and sinuous, but finally it led to what he called the rehabilitation of irreversible processes. The progresses that stand out as major landmarks of this endeavour that imposed a U-turn with respect to conceptions of classical physics deeply rooted since the nineteenth century will be described. This article is part of the theme issue ‘Dissipative structures in matter out of equilibrium: from chemistry, photonics and biology (Part 1)’.

## 1. Introduction

The dominant preoccupation at the centre of Prigogine’s work is the duality that has always existed between two theoretical descriptions: on one side, the time-reversible description of classical mechanics or of Schrödinger quantum physics and, on the other side, the irreversible evolution in time predicted by thermodynamics and its second principle. The interpretation that usually prevails concerning this duality is essentially negative in relation to irreversible phenomena. This point of view is expressed in two ways. At the macroscopic level and in practice, irreversible processes are only viewed as causes of energy degradation and of loss of useful work; at the fundamental level, the notion of irreversible evolution stemming from the second principle is only viewed as the consequence of a coarse graining approximation that ignores the complexity of the underlying microscopic dynamics of physical particles. In brief, according to this interpretation and the expression of Max Born, often criticized by Prigogine, thermodynamics results from the introduction of ignorance into physics. That ignorance, in other words the limits of human knowledge, could be at the root of a major aspect of natural processes always seemed an unbelievable, quite unsatisfactory conception to Prigogine. Convinced that important questions neglected for much too long were there, he looked all his life for a different interpretation. At the macroscopic level, he tackled the negative view against irreversible processes and, according to his own terms, rehabilitated irreversible processes by elucidating the thermodynamic conditions underlying non-equilibrium self-organization phenomena of which living matter in particular furnishes striking examples. At the microscopic level, he tried to account differently, i.e. in strictly dynamic terms excluding the stochastic ingredient introduced by Boltzmann, of the fundamental problem of statistical mechanics often described in the popular scientific literature as the mystery of the arrow of time. Finally, his aim was to show that macroscopic irreversibility is not the consequence of ignorance and approximations, but is already rooted at the microscopic level in some classes of dynamical systems. The constructive role of irreversible phenomena and the notion of time in physics are thus the two dominating research themes of his work.

This paper, based on Prigogine’s autobiography [1], is devoted to the first of these themes and the discovery of the physical mechanisms underlying non-equilibrium self-organization. Other presentations that include Prigogine’s conceptions concerning the arrow of time, situate his humanistic views on Science, his fundamentally confident optimism in regard to the future and scientific progress can be found in numerous biographies written in recent years. The most complete is the one by Radu Balescu published by the Académie royale de Belgique in 2006. It contains the most general analysis of his works and a bibliography of his more than 1000 scientific articles, books and other publications [2]. A biographical notice more particularly devoted to the works associated with the Nobel Prize for chemistry has also appeared in the Nouvelle Biographie Nationale published by the Académie royale de Belgique in 2013 [3].

## 2. Chemical thermodynamics and the molecular theory of solutions (1940–1957)

In the footsteps of Théophile De Donder, his PhD thesis director, founder of the Belgian school of thermodynamics, Ilya Prigogine published between 1940 and 1944 no fewer than 21 scientific articles. 1 At the same time, he began with Raymond Defay, 2 an older former student of De Donder, writing a Traité de thermodynamique conformément aux méthodes de Gibbs et De Donder. 3 They foresaw that it would comprise four volumes. A brief explanation of the reference made in the title to the methods of Gibbs and De Donder is useful for the following.

In classical thermodynamics, the study of equilibrium stability is mainly due to Gibbs. It is based on the thermodynamic potentials method that, as Duhem noted [5], is only applicable in special equilibrium cases where such potentials exist. To get rid of this restriction in chemistry, in 1922 De Donder succeeded in evaluating the non-compensated heat of Clausius for chemical reactions [6, 7], dividing the uncompensated heat by the temperature yields then the chemical entropy production or, more simply in everyday language, the chemical dissipation. In other words, he succeeded in transforming the expression of the second principle, which before, except at equilibrium, was only an inequality, into an equation in which all terms are evaluated whether or not one is at equilibrium. This allowed him to directly deduce from the second principle the exact physical expression of the thermodynamic chemical force, now usually called the chemical affinity, and to give a precise semi-thermodynamic, semi-kinetic definition of the conjugated thermodynamic flux, i.e. the chemical reaction rate, now usually called the De Donder equation (cf. e.g. [8]). The affinity that still was the old, intuitive, obscure notion introduced by Boerhaave of Leiden (1733) 4 with De Donder becomes a precise, clearly defined state function that both fixes the distance of chemical reactions with respect to equilibrium and their direction of evolution [6, 7]. The method of De Donder then links the study of the stability of equilibrium states to the properties of the entropy production, i.e. the non-negative expression obtained by summing the products of conjugated thermodynamic forces and fluxes. Prigogine never missed an opportunity to cite or pay tribute to this contribution of De Donder. It initiated the thermodynamic description of irreversible out of equilibrium phenomena; it unlocked the door giving access to the study of the stability of non-equilibrium stationary states.

The first two volumes of the treatise are devoted to Chemical Thermodynamics and written by Prigogine and Defay; they appeared in 1944 and 1946. In the following editions, they were combined into a single volume [9–11]. 5 The third volume devoted to Surface tension and adsorption, written by Defay and Prigogine appeared in 1951. In those texbooks, like De Donder before them, the authors are above all interested in true equilibria for which thermodynamic forces and fluxes vanish simultaneously. Some remarkable developments, however, concerning relaxation phenomena already go beyond this strictly equilibrium framework and anticipated the content of the fourth volume. In particular, the authors report a completely original analysis of the relaxation mechanism of systems the dissipation of which (entropy production) and dissipation flux (rate of reaction) tend towards zero, while the distance with respect to true equilibrium, measured by the dissipative force (affinity), stays finite and non-zero. This analysis is applied to the study of the transition towards the vitreous state, a problem of considerable importance in many fields. They establish the basic relationship controlling this transition, now known as the Prigogine–Defay configurational ratio: when the temperature is equal to the vitrification temperature, it links the difference between the vitreous state and the undercooled liquid of the isotherm compressibility, isobaric thermic dilatation coefficient and volumic isobaric specific heat.

Finally, the treatise only comprises these three volumes. Mainly devoted to equilibrium thermodynamics, they have fundamentally deepened this classical field, extended its domain of application and updated its presentation. Translated by the British physico-chemist Douglas H. Everett, FRS, they also largely made known the methods developed by the Belgian school of thermodynamics. Prigogine’s agrégation thesis, presented at the University of Brussels in 1945, was initially supposed to become the basis of the fourth volume of the treatise; finally, it was not published as such but appeared separately in 1947 [12, 13]. Before considering the content of this thesis, it is impossible to leave equilibrium thermodynamics without mentioning the contributions of Prigogine to the molecular theory of solutions.

The considerable time he devoted to the theory of solutions between 1940 and 1957 revealed the lasting influence of Jean Timmermans, an eminent experimentalist, specialist of non-ideal liquid solutions. Prigogine became his successor at a chair of chemical physics at the Université Libre de Bruxelles in 1951; his Service de Chimie Physique II created at this occasion comprised an important experimental section until the mid-1970s.

The influence of Timmermans familiarized Prigogine with the application of thermodynamics to precise physico-chemical questions directly related with experimentations. Surrounded by a first team of theoretician and experimentalists, he tackled the theoretical problem to account for the thermodynamic properties of solutions and mixtures in terms of the laws that at the microscopic level govern molecular interactions. While the theories existing at that time used extremely idealized models of matter, Prigogine developed in order to describe the liquid state and different types of interactions, the much more detailed so-called cell method [14–19].
